title: Radiation Oncology 101
question: What is radiation oncology and where does RT fit into cancer care?
html:
Before you learn any of the technical details of this rotation, it helps to have the big picture: what radiation oncology actually is, and how it fits alongside the other two pillars of cancer care. Everything else you learn on this Sub-I will hang off this framework, so it's worth having it solid before your first day.

What Radiation Oncology Actually Does

Radiation oncology is the specialty that uses high-energy radiation, usually photon beams from a machine called a linear accelerator (LINAC), to damage the DNA of cancer cells so they can no longer divide. Given enough damage, the cell dies the next time it tries to replicate. Normal cells are damaged too, but they're generally better at repairing that damage than cancer cells are, which is the whole basis for why radiation works as a cancer treatment rather than just a blunt injury (more on this in the "How Radiation Works" section).

Radiation is a local therapy. It treats the area it's aimed at and nothing else, which is a useful contrast to draw right away.

Three Pillars, Three Different Tools

Almost every cancer patient you meet this month is being managed by some combination of three specialties, each bringing a different kind of treatment to the table:

  1. Surgical oncology treats disease by physically removing it: resecting the tumor, taking out lymph nodes, or debulking bulky disease.
  2. Medical oncology treats disease with drugs that circulate through the whole body: chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, hormone therapy. This is systemic therapy, useful because cancer cells can be hiding anywhere, not just at the primary site.
  3. Radiation oncology treats disease locally, like surgery does, but with beams of radiation (or radioactive sources) instead of a scalpel. It can reach places surgery can't easily get to, and it can be used even when a patient isn't a surgical candidate.

Because these three specialties are so often treating the very same patient, most new cancer diagnoses go through some kind of multidisciplinary discussion, whether that's a formal tumor board or just three attendings reading the same chart before deciding on a plan together.

The Four Ways Radiation Gets Used

One of the first things you should get comfortable with is the vocabulary oncologists use to describe why a treatment is being given. You'll hear these words constantly on rounds and in consult notes:

  • Definitive: radiation is the main treatment meant to cure or permanently control the cancer, with no other therapy planned to follow it (though it's frequently given together with chemotherapy). Example: definitive chemoradiation for a locally advanced head and neck cancer in a patient who isn't a surgical candidate.
  • Adjuvant: radiation is given after another primary treatment (almost always surgery) to lower the risk that the cancer comes back. The visible tumor is already gone; the goal is to mop up microscopic disease that might be left behind. Example: whole breast radiation after a lumpectomy.
  • Neoadjuvant: radiation is given before another treatment, usually to shrink a tumor and make it easier (or possible) to resect, or to improve the odds surgery gets clean margins. Example: preoperative chemoradiation for rectal cancer before surgical resection.
  • Palliative: radiation is given to relieve symptoms (pain, bleeding, obstruction, neurologic compromise) rather than to cure the cancer. Example: a short course of radiation to a painful bone metastasis.

A quick way to keep these straight: ask yourself two questions about any patient. Is the goal to cure, or to control symptoms? And is anything else being done to the primary tumor, and if so, before or after the radiation? Those two questions get you to definitive, adjuvant, neoadjuvant, or palliative almost every time.

Where Radiation Fits Alongside Surgery and Systemic Therapy

You'll quickly notice that most patients don't get just one type of treatment. Some common patterns worth recognizing early:

  • Surgery, then radiation (adjuvant): common in breast cancer, and in head and neck cancers with high-risk features found at surgery.
  • Radiation and chemotherapy together, then surgery (neoadjuvant): common in rectal cancer and esophageal cancer.
  • Radiation and chemotherapy together, with no surgery at all (definitive concurrent chemoradiation): common in locally advanced lung cancer, cervical cancer, and anal cancer, and in head and neck cancers being treated with organ preservation in mind.
  • Radiation alone, often in patients who aren't candidates for surgery or intensive chemotherapy, or for tumor types where radiation alone already cures a high proportion of patients (early-stage prostate cancer, for instance).

You don't need to memorize which pattern applies to which cancer type right now. That comes with the disease-site material later in this app. For now, just recognize that the "why radiation, and why now" question almost always has an answer rooted in one of these patterns.

Who's Actually on the Rad Onc Team

Radiation oncology has more moving parts behind the scenes than most rotations you've been on, and knowing who does what will help you understand why things happen in the order they do:

  • Attending radiation oncologist: the physician who sees the patient in consult, decides on the treatment approach, prescribes the dose, and approves the final plan before treatment starts.
  • Resident: works under the attending, often does a large share of the contouring (drawing the target and organs at risk on the planning scan) and helps manage patients during treatment.
  • Medical physicist: ensures the treatment plan and the machine delivering it are safe and accurate; physically checks the plan's dose calculations before it's ever used on a patient.
  • Dosimetrist: builds the actual radiation plan (the arrangement of beams, or the "recipe") to hit the target while sparing normal tissue, usually working from the contours the physician has drawn.
  • Radiation therapist (RTT): the person who runs the CT simulation and, later, delivers each daily treatment on the machine. You will see them constantly.
  • Nurse: manages symptoms and side effects throughout treatment, and is often the first call when a patient has a problem between visits.
  • Social work, nutrition, speech-language pathology, and others get involved as needed, especially for patients going through intensive treatments like head and neck chemoradiation.

The Workflow, in One Sentence

Every patient who ends up getting radiation moves through the same basic sequence: consult, simulation, planning, and treatment. A patient is seen in consult and a decision is made to treat; they come back for a planning CT scan called a simulation; the physics and dosimetry team build a plan off that scan while the physician reviews and approves it; and then the patient returns daily (or for just a few visits) to actually receive the treatment. You'll live inside this pipeline for the whole rotation, and it's covered step by step, with everything that happens in between, in the next section, "The Radiation Treatment Journey."

High-Yield Summary
  • Radiation oncology delivers local therapy, alongside surgery (also local) and medical oncology (systemic).
  • Four treatment intents to know cold: definitive (curative, radiation is the main treatment), adjuvant (after surgery, mops up microscopic disease), neoadjuvant (before surgery, shrinks the tumor), and palliative (symptom relief, not cure).
  • The core team: attending, resident, medical physicist, dosimetrist, radiation therapist, and nurse, each with a distinct role in getting a patient from consult to treatment.
  • Every patient moves through the same basic pipeline: consult → simulation → planning → treatment.

title: Your Rad Onc Sub-I
question: What am I actually supposed to be doing?
html:
The single most common feeling on the first day of a Rad Onc Sub-I is not knowing what you're actually supposed to be doing with your time. Unlike surgery or medicine, there's no long-established script that every med student already half-knows from TV. This section is that script.

What a Typical Day Looks Like

Most Rad Onc services run on some version of this rhythm:

  1. Morning chart review: before clinic starts, the team looks through the day's patients, new consults and follow-ups alike.
  2. On-treatment visits (OTVs): brief weekly check-ins with patients currently receiving radiation, usually worked into the same clinic block.
  3. Clinic: new patient consults and follow-up visits, seen by the attending with the resident and student involved to varying degrees depending on the service's culture.
  4. Contouring and plan review time: time set aside (sometimes at the end of the day, sometimes in blocks between patients) for the attending and resident to contour new patients or review treatment plans that dosimetry has built.
  5. Occasional simulation observation: if a new patient is being simulated that day, this is worth attending if your schedule allows it.

The exact mix varies a lot by institution and even by attending, so your first move on day one should simply be to ask the resident or coordinator what the day's schedule looks like.

Before Clinic: What to Do With a New Consult

If you know you're seeing a new consult, don't walk in cold. Before the patient arrives:

  1. Read the most recent medical oncology and surgical oncology notes, if they exist, to understand what the rest of the team is already thinking.
  2. Look at the pathology report yourself: histology, grade, margins, receptor status if relevant, lymphovascular invasion.
  3. Pull up the imaging and actually look at it, not just the radiologist's impression.
  4. Try to work out the stage yourself before you see what anyone else has written.

This is covered in much more depth in "The Rad Onc Consult," but the short version is: the goal isn't to arrive with the right answer memorized, it's to arrive having already tried to think it through, so that what you learn in the room actually sticks.

During OTVs: What to Actually Do

On-treatment visits are short (often 5 to 10 minutes) but they're one of the best places for a student to be genuinely useful, because they follow a predictable pattern every time. Before the attending walks in, you can usually:

  • Ask about how the patient is tolerating treatment so far: energy, appetite, pain, and any site-specific symptoms (see "OTVs" for the full symptom list by site).
  • Do a focused exam relevant to the treatment site, especially the skin in the radiation field.
  • Check whether they've had any recent labs or imaging that need to be reviewed.

Then present a brief, focused summary to the attending before they go in, the same way you would in any other clinic.

How to Be Useful on Service

A few things reliably make a student valuable on this rotation, independent of how much radiation oncology knowledge you walk in with:

  1. Show up prepared. Read what's available on a patient before you see them; it takes ten minutes and changes how much you get out of the encounter.
  2. Take real ownership of your patients' stories. Know their oncologic history well enough to tell it without looking at the chart.
  3. Ask about the plan, not just the diagnosis. "What's the treatment plan and why" is a more useful question than "what type of cancer is this."
  4. Follow up on your patients. If you saw someone in consult, check in on how their simulation or first treatment went. This kind of continuity is memorable and genuinely appreciated.
  5. Be present and curious during contouring. Even if you aren't drawing anything yourself, watching an attending explain their reasoning while contouring is some of the highest-yield teaching time on the whole rotation.

What Residents and Attendings Actually Expect From You

Expectations on a Sub-I are almost always more about attitude and reliability than about baseline radiation oncology knowledge. In practice, that means:

  • Being on time, and communicating early if you won't be.
  • Doing the reading you're asked to do, even if it's just a few pages before the next day's patients.
  • Asking questions when you don't understand something, ideally at a natural pause rather than mid-sentence during a consult.
  • Presenting patients in an organized way (see "How to Present a Patient" for exactly what that should sound like).
  • Being honest when you don't know something, rather than guessing and hoping it lands.

What You Genuinely Don't Need to Know on Day 1

It's worth saying plainly: nobody expects you to walk in already fluent in radiobiology, physics, or contouring. You are not behind if you don't know what a DVH is yet, or can't yet explain the difference between IMRT and VMAT. That's exactly what the rest of this background section, and the disease-site modules that follow it, are for. Your job in week one is simply to learn the rhythm of the day, be a reliable presence in the room, and start building the habits above. The technical vocabulary will come quickly once you've seen it applied to real patients a few times.

High-Yield Summary
  • A typical day: chart review, OTVs, clinic (new patients and follow-ups), and contouring or plan review time. Ask on day one how your specific service structures it.
  • Before any new consult: read the med onc and surg onc notes, review pathology and imaging yourself, and try to stage the patient before you're told the answer.
  • OTVs are short but high-value: ask about tolerance and site-specific symptoms, do a focused exam, and present a tight summary before the attending walks in.
  • What actually makes you useful: preparation, ownership of your patients' stories, asking about the plan, following up over time, and staying engaged during contouring.
  • You are not expected to know radiobiology, physics, or contouring cold on day one. That knowledge builds over the rotation.

title: The Rad Onc Consult
question: How do I prepare for and conduct a consultation?
html:
The consult is where everything starts. It's also the encounter where a well-prepared student stands out the most, because so much of what makes a consult go well happens before the patient ever walks in the room. This section walks through the consult in three phases: before, during, and after.

Before the Patient: Do the Homework

Try to work through these steps, roughly in order, before you walk into the room:

  1. Read the medical oncology note (if one exists). This tells you what systemic therapy is planned or already underway, and often gives you the referring oncologist's framing of the case.
  2. Read the surgical oncology note (if one exists). This tells you what's already been resected, what margins and pathology showed, and whether further surgery is being considered.
  3. Review the pathology report yourself: histologic subtype, grade, margins, lymphovascular or perineural invasion, receptor or biomarker status if relevant to that cancer type.
  4. Review the imaging yourself, not just the written report. Pull up the actual CT, MRI, or PET and look at the primary tumor and nodal basins. This is a habit that pays off for the rest of your career, not just this month.
  5. Determine the stage yourself (TNM and overall group stage) before you see what anyone else has documented. Getting it wrong is fine and expected; the point is the attempt.
  6. Look up the relevant NCCN pathway for that cancer type and stage, so you have a rough sense of the guideline-recommended options going into the room.
  7. Identify the specific question being asked of Radiation Oncology. Is this a request to discuss adjuvant radiation? Definitive chemoradiation? A second opinion? Knowing this shapes the whole encounter.

You will not always have time to do all seven steps for every patient, especially on a busy clinic day. Even doing the first, easiest three (pathology, imaging, and identifying the clinical question) puts you well ahead of where most students start.

During the Consult: What Actually Happens in the Room

A radiation oncology consult has its own rhythm, distinct from a general medicine visit:

  • Focused oncologic history: how the diagnosis was made, the workup that followed, and every treatment received so far, in order.
  • Relevant past medical history: with an eye toward anything that could affect radiation tolerance or planning (prior radiation to a nearby area, connective tissue disease, cardiopulmonary disease, pacemakers or other implants, pregnancy status when relevant).
  • Cancer-specific physical exam: focused on the primary site and draining lymph node basins, not a full head-to-toe exam.
  • Reviewing imaging with the patient: many attendings will pull up the scan and show the patient (in plain language) what's being treated and why.
  • Discussing treatment options: radiation is presented alongside the alternatives, including the option of no further treatment, when that's a genuine choice.
  • Explaining risks and benefits: expected side effects, both short-term (during and just after treatment) and long-term, weighed against the expected benefit.
  • Assessing the patient's goals and preferences: what matters most to this particular patient. Two patients with an identical diagnosis can reasonably choose different paths.

After the Consult: Writing It Up

The consult note that follows generally closes with three things:

  1. Assessment: a concise summary of the diagnosis, stage, and clinical situation.
  2. Treatment recommendation: what's being recommended, at what intent (definitive, adjuvant, neoadjuvant, or palliative) and, where appropriate, in what sequence relative to other treatments.
  3. Next steps: what happens next logistically, most often scheduling a CT simulation, though sometimes it's obtaining additional workup first, or a plan to hold off and reassess.

As a student, you'll often be asked to write a note or a portion of one. The example below shows the kind of structure and level of detail that generally works well.

Worked Example: Radiation Oncology Consult Note

Fictional composite patient, created for teaching purposes only.

Reason for Consult

58-year-old woman referred by Surgical Oncology for consideration of adjuvant radiation following left breast lumpectomy for invasive ductal carcinoma.

History of Present Illness

Ms. R is a 58-year-old woman with no significant past medical history who first noted a palpable left breast mass on self-exam approximately six weeks ago. Diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound showed a 1.8 cm irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. Core needle biopsy confirmed invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, ER/PR positive, HER2 negative. She underwent left breast lumpectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy two weeks ago; final pathology showed a 1.7 cm invasive ductal carcinoma with clear margins (closest margin 4 mm) and 0 of 2 sentinel nodes positive for malignancy. She is now referred for consideration of adjuvant radiation therapy. She has already met with Medical Oncology, who plan to start adjuvant endocrine therapy.

Relevant Past Medical History

No prior radiation to the chest or breast. No connective tissue disease. No cardiac or pulmonary disease. No pacemaker or implanted device. Postmenopausal.

Physical Exam

Well-healed lumpectomy incision in the left upper outer breast without erythema or drainage. No palpable masses in either breast. No palpable axillary, supraclavicular, or cervical lymphadenopathy.

Imaging and Pathology Reviewed

Diagnostic mammogram and surgical pathology reviewed directly; findings as above. No evidence of multicentric disease or suspicious contralateral findings.

Staging

Pathologic stage pT1c pN0, Stage IA invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative.

Assessment

Ms. R is a 58-year-old woman status post breast-conserving surgery for Stage IA, hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, now presenting for consideration of adjuvant radiation to reduce the risk of local recurrence.

Plan

Discussed at length with the patient the role of adjuvant whole breast radiation after breast-conserving surgery, including the alternative of omitting radiation given her age and favorable tumor biology, and the expected reduction in local recurrence risk with treatment. Reviewed anticipated side effects including fatigue and skin changes, and the small long-term risks to the heart and lung. The patient wishes to proceed with adjuvant radiation. Plan for hypofractionated whole breast radiation, to be simulated with CT simulation in the treatment position using a deep inspiratory breath hold technique given left-sided treatment. Will coordinate timing with her planned endocrine therapy.

Notice what this note is doing structurally: it moves from the story (HPI), to the exam and objective findings, to a clear statement of stage, and finally to an assessment and plan that directly answers the question the consult was asked to answer. That same shape, story, then findings, then stage, then plan, is what you should be aiming for whether you're writing a note or presenting a patient out loud, which is exactly what the next section covers.

High-Yield Summary
  • Before the patient: read med onc and surg onc notes, review pathology and imaging yourself, stage the patient yourself, check the NCCN pathway, and identify the specific question being asked of Rad Onc.
  • During the consult: focused oncologic history, relevant PMH, cancer-specific exam, imaging review with the patient, discussion of options and risks/benefits, and the patient's own goals.
  • After the consult: the note closes with assessment, treatment recommendation (including intent), and next steps.
  • A good consult note tells the story, states the findings, commits to a stage, and answers the clinical question with a clear plan.

title: How to Present a Patient
question: How do I present new patients, follow-ups, and OTVs effectively?
html:
Presenting well is one of the fastest ways to build trust with an attending, and it's a completely learnable skill with a fairly fixed structure in radiation oncology. There are really three flavors of presentation you'll give on this rotation: new patient, follow-up, and OTV. Each has its own shape.

The Rule That Matters More Than Any Template

Before getting into structure, here's the single most important habit to build: don't just copy the chart. It's tempting to relay whatever the referring note says (stage, plan, and all) without doing your own thinking. Resist this. Read the imaging yourself, work out the stage yourself, and come up with your own sense of what the treatment plan should be, before you present the patient. You will sometimes be wrong, and that's fine, and expected. What attendings are actually listening for is whether you engaged with the case, not whether you arrived at the identical answer they did.

New Patient Presentations

The standard skeleton for a new patient presentation is:

  1. One-liner: age, sex, and the core diagnosis in a single sentence.
  2. Oncologic history: how the diagnosis was made and the story so far, in chronological order.
  3. Imaging: what you saw on review, not just what the report said.
  4. Pathology: histology, grade, and any relevant biomarkers.
  5. Stage: your own assessment of TNM and overall stage.
  6. Treatment history: everything done so far (surgery, chemotherapy, prior radiation).
  7. Assessment and plan: your own proposed plan, stated with appropriate humility, followed by the actual recommendation once it's been discussed.

One nuance worth knowing: how much past medical history to include depends heavily on the attending. Some want a full PMH read out every time; others only want to hear about it if it's actually relevant to radiation planning or tolerance (a prior radiation course, connective tissue disease, cardiopulmonary disease, an implanted device). If you're not sure which kind of attending you're working with, ask, or simply lead with the relevant PMH and offer to give the rest if they want it.

Worked Example: New Patient Oral Presentation

Same fictional composite patient as the consult note example.

"This is Ms. R, a 58-year-old postmenopausal woman with newly diagnosed left breast cancer, referred for consideration of adjuvant radiation after breast-conserving surgery.

She initially presented six weeks ago with a palpable left breast mass, found on diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound to be a 1.8 centimeter irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant. Core biopsy confirmed invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, ER and PR positive, HER2 negative. Two weeks ago she underwent left lumpectomy with sentinel node biopsy.

On my own review of the imaging, I didn't see any suspicious findings in the contralateral breast or any concerning axillary adenopathy. Final pathology showed a 1.7 centimeter invasive ductal carcinoma with clear margins and 0 of 2 sentinel nodes positive.

Based on that, I'd stage her as pT1c pN0, Stage IA, hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative disease.

She has no history of prior radiation, no connective tissue disease, and no cardiopulmonary disease relevant to left-sided treatment planning. She's already met with Medical Oncology, who are planning adjuvant endocrine therapy.

Given her stage and favorable biology, my leading thought was that she's a candidate for either adjuvant whole breast radiation or, given her age and tumor characteristics, a discussion about the possibility of omitting radiation altogether. I understand the plan discussed with her today was hypofractionated whole breast radiation using a breath hold technique, which she'd like to proceed with."

Follow-Up Presentations

A follow-up visit happens after treatment (or after a prior visit), so the presentation is oriented around change over time rather than a new story. The core question you're answering is simply: what has happened since the last visit? A clean way to organize that:

  1. Treatment received since the last visit (or the completed course, if this is the first follow-up after treatment).
  2. Response: how the disease looks now, based on exam and any interval imaging.
  3. Toxicity: any side effects, acute or late, and how they've evolved.
  4. New imaging, if obtained, and what it shows.
  5. Next step: continued surveillance, further workup, or a change in management.

OTV Presentations

On-treatment visits are the shortest and most repetitive presentation you'll give, which is exactly why having a tight structure matters. The standard shape:

  1. Current treatment: what they're receiving and how many fractions in (for example, "fraction 12 of 25").
  2. Symptoms: how they're feeling overall, plus anything site-specific (see the "OTVs" section for the full symptom checklist by treatment site).
  3. Toxicity: graded severity of any side effects, and whether they're worsening, stable, or improving.
  4. Exam: focused on the treatment field, especially the skin.
  5. Treatment progress: whether treatment is proceeding as planned or needs to be adjusted.
  6. Plan: continue as is, add or adjust symptom management, or, rarely, consider a treatment break.
High-Yield Summary
  • Don't just relay the chart. Read the imaging, stage the patient, and form your own plan before you present.
  • New patient: one-liner → oncologic history → imaging → pathology → stage → treatment history → assessment/plan. How much PMH to include depends on the attending.
  • Follow-up: organized around what's changed since the last visit, treatment → response → toxicity → new imaging → next step.
  • OTV: current treatment → symptoms → toxicity → exam → treatment progress → plan. Short, but keep it structured every time.

title: The Radiation Treatment Journey
question: What happens between consult and the first fraction?
html:
This is the page to come back to whenever you catch yourself thinking "wait, what happens after simulation, again?" Everything you'll see this month, from a new consult to a patient finishing their last fraction, is a step somewhere along this single pipeline. Treat it as the map, and the sections that follow (Machines, How Radiation Works, Simulation, and Contouring & Planning) as the zoomed-in detail on individual steps.

1
Consult
→
2
CT Simulation
→
3
Contouring
→
4
Treatment Planning
↓
5
Plan Review / QA
→
6
Treatment Delivery
→
7
OTVs
→
8
End of Treatment / Follow-Up

1. Consult

The patient is seen, their case is reviewed, and a decision is made about whether to treat, at what intent, and (often) with what general technique. This is covered in full in "The Rad Onc Consult."

2. CT Simulation

The patient returns for a planning CT scan, taken in the exact position they'll be treated in, often using an immobilization device to make that position reproducible day after day. This scan becomes the foundation everything else is built on. Covered in full in "Simulation 101."

3. Contouring

The physician (often with heavy resident involvement) draws, slice by slice, on the simulation CT: the target volume (the tumor and areas at risk for microscopic spread) and the organs at risk nearby that need to be protected. Covered in full in "Contouring & Treatment Planning 101."

4. Treatment Planning

Once contours are approved, a dosimetrist uses specialized software to design a plan, an arrangement of radiation beams, angles, and intensities, that delivers the prescribed dose to the target while keeping nearby organs at risk under their dose limits.

5. Plan Review and Quality Assurance

Before any plan is ever used on a patient, it's checked. The physician reviews the dose distribution against the target and organs at risk, and the medical physicist independently verifies that the plan is calculated correctly and that the machine can deliver it safely and accurately as designed.

6. Treatment Delivery

The patient returns, is set up in the same reproducible position established at simulation, and the plan is delivered. Depending on the technique, this might be a single treatment (as in SRS or SBRT) or, more commonly, one fraction a day, five days a week, over several weeks. Covered in more detail in "Radiation Machines & Modalities."

7. On-Treatment Visits (OTVs)

While a patient is actively receiving a multi-week course of radiation, they're seen at regular intervals (often weekly) to check for side effects and confirm treatment is proceeding as expected. Covered in full in "OTVs."

8. End of Treatment and Follow-Up

Once the prescribed course is complete, the patient is seen to assess how they're recovering from any acute side effects, and then re-enters a surveillance schedule: periodic visits, exams, and imaging to watch for recurrence and monitor for late side effects, which can sometimes take months to years to appear or resolve.

High-Yield Summary
  • Every patient moves through the same eight-step pipeline: consult → CT simulation → contouring → treatment planning → plan review/QA → treatment delivery → OTVs → end of treatment/follow-up.
  • Contours are drawn by the physician team; the plan itself (the beam arrangement) is built by dosimetry, then independently checked by physics before it's ever used.
  • Come back to this page any time you lose track of where a particular patient is in their course.

title: Radiation Machines & Modalities
question: What are we actually treating with?
html:
Patients will ask you what machine they're being treated on, and residents will casually drop terms like VMAT or SBRT into a presentation and assume you know what they mean. This page is meant to get you conversational, not expert, in the major machines and techniques you'll encounter. For each one, the goal is simply: what is it, when do we use it, and what does it actually look like clinically.

The LINAC: The Machine Behind Almost Everything

The linear accelerator (LINAC) is the workhorse machine of radiation oncology, and the vast majority of what you'll see this month comes out of one. It accelerates electrons and directs them at a heavy metal target, producing high-energy X-rays that are then shaped and aimed at the patient. Nearly every technique described below (3D conformal, IMRT, VMAT, SRS, SBRT) is simply a different way of using a LINAC. Clinically, it looks like a large rotating machine (a "gantry") arcing around a treatment table, with the patient lying still underneath.

3D Conformal Radiotherapy (3D-CRT)

What it is: radiation delivered from a handful of fixed beam angles, each shaped to roughly match the outline of the target from that angle.
When we use it: simpler cases where the target isn't wrapped closely around sensitive structures, and for many palliative treatments where speed and simplicity matter more than a highly sculpted dose distribution.
What it looks like clinically: a short, straightforward plan, often just a handful of beams, sometimes delivered in very few fractions for a palliative course.

Intensity-Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT)

What it is: radiation delivered from multiple fixed angles, but with the intensity of the beam varied across each field using a device called a multileaf collimator, allowing the dose to be sculpted much more precisely around an irregularly shaped target.
When we use it: targets sitting close to critical structures, most classically head and neck cancer, where the target often wraps around the spinal cord, parotid glands, and other organs that need to be spared.
What it looks like clinically: longer, more complex treatment plans and appointments, and a plan that goes through a more involved quality assurance process before it's used.

Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy (VMAT)

What it is: a further evolution of IMRT in which the gantry rotates continuously around the patient while simultaneously modulating beam intensity, rather than stopping at fixed angles.
When we use it: most of the same situations as IMRT; VMAT has largely become the default modern technique at many centers because it can deliver a similarly sculpted dose distribution more quickly.
What it looks like clinically: a treatment session where the machine rotates smoothly around the patient rather than stopping and starting at each angle, generally making for a faster appointment than older IMRT.

Stereotactic Radiosurgery (SRS)

What it is: very high, precisely focused doses of radiation delivered to a small target, in a single treatment or just a few. "Radiosurgery" is a bit of a historical name; no incision is involved.
When we use it: almost always intracranial targets, most commonly brain metastases, given in one fraction with extremely tight margins around the target.
What it looks like clinically: a single appointment (sometimes a very long one), with extensive imaging and setup verification beforehand given how little room for error there is.

Stereotactic Body Radiotherapy (SBRT / SABR)

What it is: the same basic concept as SRS (high dose, tight margins, very few fractions) applied outside the brain.
When we use it: small, well-defined tumors in the lung, liver, spine, or bone, particularly in patients who aren't surgical candidates, or for oligometastatic disease (a small, limited number of metastases).
What it looks like clinically: typically 1 to 5 total treatments, each appointment longer than a standard fraction because of the extra imaging and setup precision required, sometimes with implanted fiducial markers or breath-hold techniques to manage motion.

Proton Therapy

What it is: instead of X-rays, protons are used to deliver dose. Protons have a unique physical property (the "Bragg peak") that lets them deposit most of their energy at a specific depth and then stop, with very little dose continuing beyond the target. This is covered more in "How Radiation Works."
When we use it: situations where minimizing dose beyond the target matters most, classically pediatric cancers (to protect a growing body from unnecessary radiation exposure) and certain tumors near critical structures, like some CNS and skull base tumors.
What it looks like clinically: only available at specialized centers with proton facilities, so it's not something every patient has access to; when used, the workflow otherwise looks similar to photon treatment.

Brachytherapy

What it is: instead of aiming radiation at the patient from outside the body, a radioactive source is placed directly inside or immediately next to the tumor.
When we use it: classically cervical cancer (an applicator placed in the uterus and vagina) and prostate cancer (permanently implanted seeds), where it allows a very high dose right at the tumor with a steep falloff to nearby normal tissue.
What it looks like clinically: a procedure, often done under anesthesia or sedation, to place the applicator or source, which is a meaningfully different experience for the patient than the daily walk-in appointments of external beam treatment.

High-Yield Summary
  • Almost everything runs off a LINAC. 3D-CRT, IMRT, and VMAT are all different ways of shaping and delivering a photon beam from that same machine.
  • IMRT and VMAT sculpt dose around irregular targets near critical structures (classic example: head and neck); VMAT does this with a continuously rotating gantry rather than fixed angles.
  • SRS (intracranial) and SBRT/SABR (everywhere else) deliver very high doses in just 1 to 5 fractions to small, well-defined targets.
  • Protons stop depositing dose beyond the target (the Bragg peak), useful in pediatrics and near critical structures. Brachytherapy places the radioactive source directly at the tumor, classically for cervical and prostate cancer.

title: How Radiation Works
question: Why does radiation actually work?
html:
You do not need to relearn physics or cell biology to succeed on this rotation. What you need is just enough of a mental model to understand what you're actually looking at when someone shows you a plan, and enough vocabulary to follow a conversation about why one technique was chosen over another. This page is deliberately short. If you want the deeper, exam-level version of this material (the kind of detail that shows up in pimping questions), the Overview flashcard deck covers it in much more depth.

Part One: Radiobiology, the Short Version

Radiation kills cancer cells mainly by damaging their DNA badly enough that the cell can't successfully divide again. Here's the minimum you need:

  • DNA damage is the mechanism of cell kill. A double-strand break (both strands of the DNA helix broken at the same location) is the kind of damage most likely to actually kill a cell, because it's the hardest to repair accurately.
  • Direct vs. indirect damage: radiation can break DNA directly, but more often (especially with the X-rays used in most treatment), it works indirectly, by generating free radicals from water molecules in the cell, which then go on to damage the DNA.
  • Fractionation is the practice of splitting the total radiation dose into many smaller daily treatments instead of one large one. This is done because it gives normal, healthy cells time to repair damage between fractions, while cancer cells are generally worse at repairing that same damage. Spreading treatment out over time also lets the tumor reoxygenate (see below) and lets cells redistribute into more radiosensitive phases of the cell cycle between fractions.
  • Reoxygenation matters because well-oxygenated cells are more sensitive to radiation than hypoxic (oxygen-poor) ones. As a tumor shrinks over the course of treatment, previously hypoxic cells at the tumor's center gain better blood supply and become more radiosensitive, which is one of the reasons fractionated treatment works as well as it does.
  • Repopulation is the tumor's ability to keep growing back between fractions. This is part of why treatment courses shouldn't be needlessly prolonged or interrupted; giving a tumor extra time between fractions gives it extra time to regrow.
  • Radiosensitivity varies by tissue and by tumor type; you'll hear tumors and organs described as "radiosensitive" or "radioresistant" based on how much dose it takes to control or damage them.

Together, these ideas ("the four R's": repair, reoxygenation, repopulation, and redistribution) are the biological justification for why we don't just deliver one enormous dose of radiation and call it a day.

Part Two: Basic Physics, the Short Version

A few terms you'll hear constantly, worth being comfortable with even without the underlying math:

  • Dose is measured in Gray (Gy), and represents the amount of radiation energy actually absorbed by tissue.
  • Fraction is a single treatment session; a "fraction" and a daily treatment appointment are the same thing. A prescription might read something like "50 Gy in 25 fractions," meaning 2 Gy delivered per day, five days a week, for five weeks.
  • Energy refers to how penetrating the beam is; higher-energy beams travel deeper into tissue before depositing most of their dose, which is why deeper tumors are typically treated with higher-energy beams than very superficial ones.
  • Beam is simply the path radiation travels along from the machine to the patient; a plan is built from some number of beams, aimed from different angles, that overlap at the target.
  • Isodose lines are lines drawn on a plan connecting points that receive the same dose, similar to elevation lines on a topographic map. They're how you visually read a plan: tightly packed isodose lines around the target and rapidly falling off outside it indicate a well-sculpted plan.
  • Why different techniques give different dose distributions: a simple plan using a few fixed beams (3D-CRT) tends to produce a dose distribution that's less tightly wrapped around an irregular target than a plan using many beam angles and intensity modulation (IMRT/VMAT), because more angles and more modulation give the planning software more ways to cancel out dose outside the target while reinforcing it inside.

That's genuinely most of what you need for day-to-day fluency. The rest (photon interaction physics, the mathematics of biologically effective dose, and so on) is worth knowing eventually, and it's all in the Overview flashcard deck when you're ready for it, but it isn't necessary for functioning well on this rotation.

High-Yield Summary
  • Radiation kills cells mainly through DNA double-strand breaks, most often produced indirectly via free radicals rather than direct DNA hits.
  • We fractionate treatment because of the four R's: repair (normal tissue recovers between fractions better than tumor does), reoxygenation (hypoxic tumor cells become more sensitive as the tumor shrinks), repopulation (a reason not to needlessly prolong treatment), and redistribution (cells cycle into more sensitive phases between fractions).
  • Dose is measured in Gray (Gy); a treatment course is described as a total dose split into a number of fractions.
  • Isodose lines are how you read a plan visually: tight lines hugging the target with a sharp falloff outside it mean a well-shaped plan.

title: Simulation 101
question: How do we set the patient up to receive radiation accurately?
html:
Simulation is the step where a treatment plan starts to become something concrete. If you only remember one idea from this page, make it this: everything about simulation exists in service of one goal, reproducibility. The patient needs to be positioned in a way that can be recreated, exactly, every single day of treatment, sometimes for six or seven weeks in a row.

1
Patient
→
2
Immobilization
→
3
CT Scan
→
4
Treatment Position

CT Simulation: What It Actually Is

The patient lies on a flat table (the same style of table used on the actual treatment machine) inside a CT scanner dedicated to radiation oncology planning. The resulting scan is the foundation for everything downstream: contouring, planning, and daily treatment setup all reference this one scan.

Immobilization: Building a Reproducible Position

To make sure the patient is in the exact same position every day, a variety of custom devices are used depending on treatment site:

  • Thermoplastic masks for head and neck and brain treatment: a mesh-like sheet is heated until pliable, molded to the patient's face and shoulders, and then hardens as it cools, creating a custom-fit mask that clips down to the table.
  • Body molds or "vac-lok" bags for chest, abdomen, and pelvis treatment: a bag filled with beads is molded around the patient's body and then vacuum-sealed to hold that exact shape.
  • Knee and ankle supports, arm boards, and breast boards for site-specific positioning, ensuring the same limb position or body angle is recreated daily.

Whatever device is used, it's built once at simulation and then reused for every treatment fraction that follows.

Positioning

The patient is set up in the exact position they'll be treated in, which is not always the most comfortable or intuitive position. Arms may be raised overhead, the neck extended, or the body angled in a specific way, all chosen to keep the beams' paths clear of unnecessary normal tissue or to make daily setup easier to verify.

Contrast

IV or oral contrast is sometimes given during simulation to better visualize the tumor and surrounding structures on the planning CT, similar to how contrast is used in diagnostic imaging. Not every simulation uses contrast; it depends on the treatment site and what's needed to see the target clearly.

Image Fusion

The simulation CT is often merged, or "fused," with other imaging the patient has already had: a diagnostic MRI, a PET scan, or prior imaging from surgery. This lets the physician contour the target using the best available imaging for that structure (MRI for soft tissue detail in the brain, for example) while still building the actual plan on the CT, which is required for the dose calculations to be accurate.

Isocenter and Reference Marks

Once the patient's position and the target are established, a single reference point called the isocenter is defined, generally at or near the center of the target. Small marks, sometimes temporary ink, sometimes tiny permanent tattoos, are placed on the patient's skin aligned to this point using lasers in the simulation room. These marks are what the radiation therapists line up to the room's lasers every day at treatment to make sure the patient is positioned correctly before any dose is delivered.

Simulation CT vs. Diagnostic CT

It's worth explicitly noting how these differ, since patients (and sometimes you) might wonder why another CT is needed if one was already done for diagnosis. A simulation CT is done in the treatment position, with immobilization devices in place, on a flat table matching the treatment machine, specifically so it can be used to plan and verify treatment. A diagnostic CT is optimized for image quality and typically done in a generic, comfortable position, without any of that setup, and can't be substituted for planning purposes.

Why Reproducibility Is the Whole Point

Every piece of the simulation process, immobilization, positioning, and reference marks, exists to solve the same underlying problem: a treatment plan is only as good as the team's ability to recreate the exact position it was designed for, day after day, often for weeks. A few millimeters of difference in setup can matter, especially with the more tightly sculpted modern techniques described in "Radiation Machines & Modalities." This is also why image guidance (checking the patient's position with imaging right before each treatment) is used throughout the treatment course, not just at simulation.

High-Yield Summary
  • Simulation exists to solve one problem: making the patient's position reproducible every single day of treatment.
  • Immobilization devices (thermoplastic masks, vac-lok bags, and site-specific supports) are custom-built at simulation and reused for every fraction.
  • The simulation CT is done in the actual treatment position, unlike a diagnostic CT, and is often fused with MRI or PET to help define the target.
  • The isocenter and its skin marks are what get lined up to the room's lasers before every single treatment.

title: Contouring & Treatment Planning 101
question: How do we turn a diagnosis into a radiation plan?
html:
Contouring and planning are where a diagnosis on a page turns into an actual, deliverable radiation treatment. It's easy to get lost in acronyms here, so before anything else, hold onto this mental model, because it matters far more than memorizing definitions:

What are we trying to treat? What margin do we need around it? What do we need to protect nearby? Can we build a plan that covers the target while respecting those normal tissue limits?

Every contouring and planning decision on this rotation is, at its core, an attempt to answer those four questions. Here's the vocabulary that goes with each part of that process.

Target Volumes: Answering "What Are We Treating, and With What Margin?"

Target volumes are drawn as a series of nested structures, each one adding a margin for a different kind of uncertainty:

  1. GTV (gross tumor volume): the tumor you can actually see or feel, on imaging or exam. This is the starting point.
  2. CTV (clinical target volume): the GTV plus a margin for microscopic disease that isn't visible on imaging but is still assumed to be there, based on how that particular cancer type tends to spread.
  3. ITV (internal target volume): the CTV plus a margin to account for internal organ motion, most relevant for tumors that move with breathing, like lung tumors.
  4. PTV (planning target volume): the outermost margin, added to account for daily setup uncertainty, the small, unavoidable variability in how precisely the patient can be positioned each day.

A useful way to remember the order: each volume answers "what else do I need to cover, given a specific source of uncertainty," moving outward from the visible tumor to the volume that actually gets prescribed a dose.

Organs at Risk: Answering "What Do We Need to Protect?"

An organ at risk (OAR) is any normal structure near the target that could be damaged by radiation and needs to be considered during planning. OARs matter because radiation doesn't distinguish between tumor and normal tissue on its own; it's the plan's job to spare normal structures as much as possible while still covering the target. Some of the most common OARs you'll hear about in head and neck cancer specifically, since it's one of the most anatomically crowded and OAR-dense sites: the spinal cord, brainstem, parotid glands (protecting these helps prevent permanent dry mouth), mandible, and larynx (when it isn't the target itself). Every disease site has its own characteristic set of OARs, covered in the disease-site modules.

Treatment Planning: Answering "Can We Actually Build This Plan?"

Once target volumes and OARs are contoured, dosimetry builds a plan and the whole team evaluates it using a shared vocabulary:

  • Dose distribution: how the prescribed dose is actually spread across the treated area, visualized using isodose lines (see "How Radiation Works" for more on these).
  • Coverage: whether the target volume is actually receiving the prescribed dose throughout its entirety, not just in the middle.
  • Conformity: how tightly the high-dose region hugs the shape of the target, versus spilling unnecessarily into surrounding normal tissue.
  • Hotspots: small areas within or near the target receiving a higher dose than intended; some degree of hotspot is often unavoidable and acceptable, but large or poorly placed hotspots are a problem.
  • DVH (dose-volume histogram): a graph, used constantly in plan review, that shows what percentage of a given structure's volume is receiving at least a given dose. This is how a physician efficiently checks, for example, "is too much of the parotid gland getting too much dose," without needing to scroll through every CT slice.
  • OAR constraints: dose limits for organs at risk, generally based on established data about how much dose a given organ can tolerate before the risk of a specific side effect becomes unacceptably high. Plans are built and adjusted to try to stay under these limits wherever the target's coverage isn't compromised.

Putting It Together

When you watch an attending review a plan, what looks like a fast, almost intuitive glance at a screen is actually them running through that same four-question framework: is the target (GTV/CTV/PTV) adequately covered, are the OARs within acceptable limits on the DVH, is the plan reasonably conformal without unnecessary hotspots, and does all of that add up to a plan worth approving. If you can follow along with that same set of questions, you'll get far more out of plan review sessions than if you're trying to remember what every acronym stands for in the moment.

High-Yield Summary
  • The mental model that matters most: what are we treating, what margin does it need, what do we need to protect, and can we build a plan that does both?
  • Target volumes nest outward: GTV (visible tumor) → CTV (adds a margin for microscopic disease) → ITV (adds a margin for internal motion) → PTV (adds a margin for daily setup uncertainty).
  • OARs are normal structures near the target that need protecting; every disease site has its own characteristic set.
  • Plans are judged on coverage (does the target get its dose), conformity (how tightly dose hugs the target), hotspots (unwanted areas of extra dose), and the DVH (the graph used to check OAR doses against their constraints).

title: OTVs
question: How do we evaluate and manage patients during treatment?
html:
On-treatment visits are short, frequent, and deeply practical, which makes them one of the best places on this rotation to feel useful quickly. This page keeps things clinical and organized around three questions: what to ask, what to look for, and what to do about it.

What to Ask

A good OTV starts with a quick general check-in, then narrows to symptoms specific to the treatment site:

  • General: How are you feeling overall? How's your energy? Fatigue is close to universal during radiation and worth asking about even when it isn't the presenting complaint.
  • Pain: Any new or worsening pain, and is it controlled with the current regimen?
  • Nausea: Especially relevant for upper abdominal, pelvic, or whole-brain treatment, or when concurrent chemotherapy is involved.
  • Skin changes: Any redness, itching, peeling, or breakdown in the treatment field?
  • Mucositis: For head and neck patients especially, ask directly about mouth or throat pain, and about difficulty with saliva.
  • Swallowing: Any new difficulty swallowing solids or liquids, again particularly relevant for head and neck and thoracic/esophageal treatment.
  • Nutrition and hydration: Is oral intake holding up? Any weight loss? Are they able to stay hydrated?
  • Bowel and bladder symptoms: For pelvic treatment, ask specifically about diarrhea, urinary frequency, urgency, or burning with urination.

Which of these matter most depends heavily on treatment site; a patient receiving pelvic radiation and a patient receiving whole-brain radiation are being screened for almost entirely different toxicity profiles, even though the visit structure is identical.

What to Look For

Beyond what the patient tells you, a focused exam and a look at their overall trajectory matters:

  • Treatment-related toxicity on exam, most visibly skin changes in the radiation field, ranging from mild erythema to more significant desquamation.
  • Weight changes over the course of treatment, which can be an early, objective sign that oral intake or overall tolerance is declining.
  • Performance status, meaning a general sense of how well the patient is functioning day to day, not just how they say they feel in the moment.
  • Mucositis, visible on oral exam in head and neck patients, generally graded by severity.
  • Treatment response, when appropriate to assess (for instance, a shrinking palpable mass), though formal response assessment is usually done with imaging after treatment is complete rather than during it.

What to Do

The plan coming out of an OTV usually falls into one of a few buckets:

  1. Continue treatment as planned, the most common outcome when symptoms are mild and expected for where the patient is in their course.
  2. Symptom management: starting or adjusting medications for pain, nausea, or skin care, or reinforcing supportive measures already in place.
  3. Medications: this might mean a topical agent for skin toxicity, a "magic mouthwash" or topical anesthetic for mucositis, an antiemetic, or a bowel regimen, depending on the symptom.
  4. Labs: checked when clinically indicated, for example monitoring blood counts in a patient receiving concurrent chemotherapy, or basic metabolic panels in a patient with poor oral intake.
  5. Nutrition support: a referral to a dietitian, or a discussion about supplemental nutrition, if intake is becoming a real problem.
  6. IV fluids, for patients who are becoming dehydrated and can't adequately correct this with oral intake alone.
  7. Treatment break, which is relatively uncommon and generally avoided when possible, since unplanned gaps in treatment can allow the tumor extra time to repopulate (see "How Radiation Works"). It's reserved for situations where continuing treatment would be unsafe.

As a student, you won't be the one deciding which of these to pursue, but understanding the menu of options helps you anticipate what the attending is likely to ask about or order, and lets you present a more complete, useful picture of how the patient is doing.

High-Yield Summary
  • Ask both general questions (energy, pain, nausea) and site-specific ones (skin, mucositis, swallowing, GI/GU symptoms) tailored to what's actually in the treatment field.
  • Look for toxicity on exam, weight trends, and overall performance status, not just what the patient reports.
  • Most OTVs end in "continue as planned," with symptom management layered in as needed; treatment breaks are the exception, not the rule, since they give the tumor extra time to repopulate.
